desc:
Each element [start, end) of intervals is a half-open stretch of the number line: it covers every point x with start ≤ x < end, so its length is end - start. The intervals come in no particular order and may overlap, nest or repeat.

Return the total length of the number line that is covered by at least one interval. Every point must be counted once, no matter how many intervals cover it.

intervals = [[1, 5], [3, 8], [10, 12]]
result    = 9

The first two intervals together cover [1, 8), which has length 7, and the last one adds 2 more. Two intervals that only meet, such as [1, 3) and [3, 5), simply add up to 4.
hints: Adding up all lengths over-counts every point that lies in more than one interval. You need a way to count each point once.
Sort the intervals by start. Then the part of an interval that is already covered by earlier intervals is exactly the part to the left of the furthest end seen so far.
Keep reach, the largest end seen so far (start at 0). For each interval with end > reach, add end - max(start, reach) and set reach = end; intervals with end ≤ reach add nothing.
editorial: After sorting by start, process the intervals from left to right and remember reach, the right-most point covered so far. The new part contributed by an interval is the portion lying beyond reach, which has length end - max(start, reach) when end > reach and nothing otherwise. Afterwards reach becomes the new end. Each point of the line is counted exactly once, in the first interval (in sorted order) that reaches it.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan is linear. The same result comes from merging overlapping intervals first and summing the lengths of the merged blocks, but the running reach avoids building the merged list. The answer is at most 109, so it fits in 32 bits.
